subject: Chemistry
title: Carotenoids: Flamingos and Carrots
description: A micro-lesson that makes Carotenoids: Flamingos and Carrots usable.

hook.text: Flamingos are born gray. They turn pink because they eat shrimp full of carotenoid pigments that accumulate in their feathers.

buildup.text: Carotenoids are long-chain molecules with alternating double bonds. This conjugated system absorbs blue-green light.

discovery.text: Beta-carotene in carrots absorbs blue-green light and reflects orange. Your body splits it into retinol for vision.

twist.text: Eat enough carrots and your skin turns orange—a harmless condition called carotenodermia. The pigment deposits in your skin.

climax.text: Autumn leaves turn red from anthocyanins, but the yellow and orange colors were always there—masked by green chlorophyll.

punchline.text: You are what you eat—literally. Flamingos turn pink from shrimp pigments.

quiz.question: Why are flamingos pink?
options: Carotenoid pigments from their shrimp diet accumulate in their feathers
A genetic mutation produces pink melanin in flamingos
Flamingos secrete a pink oil that coats their feathers

details.summary: Carotenoids are organic pigments with long conjugated double-bond chains that absorb blue and green light, producing yellow, orange, and red colors. Flamingos are pink because they accumulate carotenoids from the shrimp and algae in their diet.
details.whyItMatters: Carotenoids are the most widespread natural pigments, coloring everything from autumn leaves to egg yolks. Beta-carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, making it essential for human nutrition.
takeaways: Long conjugated chains in carotenoids absorb blue-green light
Flamingos acquire their pink color entirely from dietary carotenoids
Beta-carotene is a precursor to vitamin A essential for vision

faq.question: Why do flamingos lose their pink color in captivity?
faq.answer: Without access to carotenoid-rich shrimp and algae, flamingos gradually lose their pink coloration as old feathers are replaced. Zoos supplement diets with canthaxanthin or similar carotenoids to maintain the characteristic pink plumage.

faq.question: Can eating too many carrots actually turn your skin orange?
faq.answer: Yes. Excessive carotenoid consumption causes carotenemia, a condition where excess beta-carotene deposits in the skin's fat layer. The palms, soles, and nasolabial folds turn noticeably yellow-orange. The condition is harmless and reverses when intake decreases.
